title: Revisiting Occupational Segregation and the Valuation of Women’s Work
affiliations: International Labour Organization (ILO) and

detail.title: Revisiting Occupational Segregation and the Valuation of Women’s Work

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: While population ageing increases the demand for care work, new technologies, including AI, reinforce the importance of human interaction, with recent research finding significant wage premiums for social skills. Against this background, we investigate two factors behind the gender wage gap: occupational gender segregation and lower pay in female-dominated occupations, especially care work, where social skills are central. Using 1972-2024 CPS data, we show that occupational gender segregation remains pronounced in the United States, with many care occupations remaining female-dominated. This continues to correlate with lower wages. Conditional on observable characteristics, a 1 percentage point increase in the occupational share of women during 2015-24 was associated with a wage decrease of 0.22 percent for women and 0.20 percent for men. We then analyze whether returns to social skills are distorted in the care sector, where we hypothesize that the wage returns on workers' performance are lower due to the public-goods aspect of care work. Based on combined CPS and O*Net data, we investigate occupation-level skills returns for 2015-24. They are indeed insignificant for care workers but sizeable for business services workers.

title: Exposure to Inequality, Human Capital Investment, and Labor Market Outcome
affiliations: Centre for Monetary and Financial Studies (CEMFI), Lund University, Lund University and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Exposure to Inequality, Human Capital Investment, and Labor Market Outcome

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We estimate the effects of exposure to income and wealth inequality during adolescence on long-term educational and labor market outcomes. Using detailed Swedish register data covering all students completing compulsory education between 1989 and 2013, we construct measures of inequality among students school-cohort peers and exploit variation between cohorts within schools to identify causal effects of inequality exposure. We find no evidence that exposure to inequality affects GPA, high school graduation, university enrollment, university completion, or income up to age 35. These null results are precisely estimated and robust to alternative measures of inequality, sample definitions, and specifications. Moreover, we find no evidence of systematic heterogeneity by socioeconomic background. Taken together, these findings suggest that school integration policies mixing students from different socioeconomic backgrounds do not necessarily carry hidden long-run costs stemming from exposure to inequality. More broadly, they challenge the view that school-based exposure to peer inequality during adolescence is a causal driver of human capital accumulation or later-life mobility.

affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University and Pusan National University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Cross-subsidization Pricing by Multiproduct Retailers: Some Evidence from U.S. Scanner Data

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: When consumers buy multiple products at a store, retailers have an incentive to price items strategically based on how each product's price affects the sales of others. Such an incentive may manifest in the form of cross-subsidization: stores use low prices on some products to attract customers, expecting to profit from high prices (or margins) on others. That is, the latter products cross-subsidize the former. We empirically examine key theories of cross-subsidization pricing using large-scale retailer scanner data from two years, 2006 and 2016. The year 2006 represents a period when consumers primarily shopped in brick-and-mortar stores, as assumed in theoretical models. Our main findings are twofold. First, in both years, large, full-line stores exhibit a pricing pattern where lower advertised prices are accompanied by higher unadvertised prices, consistent with Lal and Matutes (1994). Second, in 2006, large stores facing competition from small, limited-line stores tend to widen the price gap between less and more competitive products more than those that do not. This aligns with Chen and Rey's (2012) characterization of cross-subsidization, where multistop shoppers effectively subsidize one-stop shoppers. Together, these findings highlight cross-subsidization as an important element of retail pricing strategy and provide empirical support for existing theories.

title: The Shopper Schism: Structural Disaggregation of Consumer and Shopper in AI-Mediated Commerce

detail.title: The Shopper Schism: Structural Disaggregation of Consumer and Shopper in AI-Mediated Commerce
detail.abstract:
For over a century, commercial theory and practice have rested on a foundational assumption: the consumer who desires a product and the shopper who executes the purchase are the same human actor. This unity of intent and execution has shaped every framework from the marketing funnel to customer journey mapping, from brand-building theory to sales force management. That assumption is now breaking apart.

The emergence of autonomous AI purchasing agents—algorithms capable of independently evaluating, selecting, and transacting on behalf of human users—creates what we term the Shopper Schism: the permanent, structural disaggregation of consumer (the human who consumes) and shopper (the algorithm that purchases). This disaggregation is not a temporary technological curiosity but a fundamental restructuring of commercial relationships that invalidates core assumptions underlying modern marketing and strategic theory.

This paper applies established principal-agent theory to analyze this transformation. We demonstrate that the consumer-agent relationship exhibits classic agency problems—information asymmetry, goal misalignment, and moral hazard—but with distinctive characteristics arising from the non-human nature of the agent and the platform economics surrounding it. Through conceptual analysis grounded in emerging empirical research and illustrated with mini-case studies (Amazon Subscribe & Save, Tesla in-car purchasing), we develop five core propositions that explain how and why algorithmic intermediation fundamentally alters commercial dynamics.

We introduce the concept of the Gulf of Delegation—the expanding gap between human intent (what consumers want) and algorithmic execution (what agents purchase)—and demonstrate why this gulf cannot be eliminated through better technology but represents an inherent structural feature of delegated commerce. The paper concludes with implications for marketing theory, strategic management, and public policy, positioning the Shopper Schism as the defining challenge for commerce in the algorithmic age.

title: The Trust Paradox in AI-Mediated Commerce: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda

detail.title: The Trust Paradox in AI-Mediated Commerce: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda

declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: The emergence of autonomous AI purchasing agents represents a structural reconfiguration of commercial exchange that fundamentally alters the mechanisms and dynamics of consumer trust. This paper develops a predictive conceptual framework for understanding trust evolution in AI-mediated commerce, arguing that platforms deploying these agents will face powerful economic pressures to introduce monetization strategies that systematically erode the initial trust foundation. Drawing on principal-agent theory and the historical precedent of Google Search’s transformation from information utility to advertising platform, I propose that AI commerce will likely follow a similar trajectory absent deliberate countermeasures. The paper presents a three-phase trust lifecycle model: (1) utility-driven adoption, (2) monetization-induced misalignment, and (3) potential disillusionment and market bifurcation. I introduce the concept of “computational trust”—trust mechanisms emphasizing radical verifiability, systemic reliability, and algorithmic transparency—as a strategic response for organizations and policymakers seeking to prevent or mitigate trust erosion. The framework yields eleven testable propositions and provides strategic guidance for firms navigating the transition to agent-intermediated markets. This analysis contributes to marketing theory by extending principal-agent frameworks to three-party consumer-agent-platform relationships and by identifying computational trust as a distinct construct from traditional relationship-based trust mechanisms. As a conceptual framework developed prior to widespread AI agent deployment, this work generates testable propositions requiring empirical validation as the technology matures.

title: From Persuasion to Computation: Reconceptualizing Marketing in Agent-Mediated Markets

detail.title: From Persuasion to Computation: Reconceptualizing Marketing in Agent-Mediated Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
For over 125 years, the marketing funnel-rooted in the AIDA model (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action)-has served as the dominant paradigm for understanding consumer purchase behavior. This conceptual framework, developed during the era of mass advertising, assumes a human consumer progressing through sequential psychological stages from product awareness to final purchase. We argue that the emergence of agentic commerce-economic transactions mediated by autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of consumers-fundamentally invalidates this paradigm. AI agents possess no psychological journey; they cannot be made "aware" through advertising, develop "interest" via storytelling, or feel "desire" through emotional branding. Instead, these algorithmic intermediaries execute logical, deterministic processes that bear no resemblance to human decision-making.

This paper introduces an alternative theoretical framework: the API Call Model. Rather than psychological persuasion, agent-mediated commerce operates through three computational phases: Query (structured data requests to multiple sources), Analysis (systematic attribute comparison against objective functions), and Execution (automated transaction completion). We develop seven propositions examining how this architectural shift transforms marketing from a persuasion discipline centered on human psychology to an engineering discipline centered on machine-readable data infrastructure. Our framework challenges fundamental assumptions in marketing theory regarding the nature of consumer decision-making, the role of brands, and the mechanisms of competitive advantage in increasingly algorithm-mediated markets.

title: All Eyes on the Nerd? The Unequal Distribution of Teachers' Attention
affiliations: Brookings Institution - Economic Studies Program, Monash University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: All Eyes on the Nerd? The Unequal Distribution of Teachers' Attention

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Teachers play a central role in shaping how students benefit from peers, yet little is known about how classroom composition affects their attention-allocation decisions. We conduct a large-scale randomized experiment using realistic class- room vignettes to assess how teachers engage with students under varying scenarios and objectives. The presence of a high achiever reduces the likelihood that teachers engage with a low achiever by about 8%, with substantially larger effects when teachers prioritize task success, consistent with convenience-based decision-making. Using administrative data, we show that low achievers perform worse when quasi-randomly assigned to a classroom with an exceptional student.

title: The Great Decoupling: How Autonomous AI Agents Are Dismantling the Direct Brand-Consumer Relationship

detail.title: The Great Decoupling: How Autonomous AI Agents Are Dismantling the Direct Brand-Consumer Relationship

declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
The direct brand-consumer relationship has been the organizing principle of marketing strategy for over a century. This paper challenges that foundational assumption by examining how autonomous AI agents—acting as independent commercial intermediaries—are fundamentally restructuring market architecture. We introduce "The Great Decoupling" as a conceptual framework to explain the systematic severance of transactional, informational, and communicative links between brands and consumers through AI intermediation.

Drawing on transaction cost economics, disintermediation theory, and principal-agent frameworks, we model how AI agents transform market structure from a dyadic (brand-consumer) to a triadic (brand-agent-human) relationship. We demonstrate three distinct mechanisms of decoupling: (1) transactional decoupling through tokenized payment credentials that route financial flows through agents, (2) data decoupling as agents capture and sequester behavioral and preference data that previously flowed to brands, and (3) communicative decoupling as agents filter marketing messages through algorithmic logic rather than human psychology.

This framework explains why dominant strategic models—Customer Relationship Management, traditional loyalty programs, and pure Direct-to-Consumer approaches—face obsolescence. These strategies were optimized for direct human interaction and fail when purchasing decisions are delegated to computational agents operating with pure System 2 rationality.

We propose "Agent Optimality" as a new strategic paradigm where competitive advantage flows from being the mathematically optimal choice for algorithmic decision-makers rather than building emotional loyalty with humans. This requires excellence across four dimensions: comprehensive product data architectures, operational reliability, verifiable brand integrity, and deep platform integration.

The paper contributes a novel theoretical framework for analyzing AI's structural impact on markets and provides critical implications for firms navigating the transition to agent-mediated commerce. We conclude with an empirical research agenda to validate this framework as agentic commerce matures.

title: AI Shopping Agents are Psychologically American: Evidence of WEIRD Bias in Large Language Models and Implications for Global Commerce

detail.title: AI Shopping Agents are Psychologically American: Evidence of WEIRD Bias in Large Language Models and Implications for Global Commerce

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
AI shopping agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are projected to mediate trillions of dollars in global commerce by 2030, yet these systems encode Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) cultural biases that systematically disadvantage 85% of humanity (Henrich et al., 2010; Henrich, 2020). Drawing on cultural psychology and recent empirical findings that LLMs exhibit WEIRD psychological profiles (Atari et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2024), we develop the concept of "Cultural Commerce Fairness" and demonstrate that current agentic commerce architectures will fail non-WEIRD consumers through culturally-mismatched decision heuristics, trust signals, and preference structures.

We outline a multi-phase empirical research program testing nine LLMs—five US-trained models (Claude, GPT-4, Gemini, Grok, Perplexity) and four Chinese-trained models (DeepSeek, Qwen, ERNIE, GLM)—on 262 World Values Survey variables across 65 nations. We hypothesize that US models will cluster near WEIRD populations (replicating Atari et al.'s findings) while Chinese models will exhibit reversed patterns, clustering near East Asian populations. These results will validate whether training data geography determines LLM cultural psychology and establish empirical foundations for commerce fairness frameworks.

This paper makes three contributions: (1) theoretical framework connecting cultural psychology to algorithmic commerce, (2) research design for systematic cultural bias measurement in commercial AI systems, and (3) policy recommendations for cultural fairness standards. Our forthcoming empirical papers will test whether AI shopping agents encode culturally-specific decision-making that advantages WEIRD consumers at the expense of the global majority, with profound implications for digital commerce equity and AI governance.

title: Does Differentiation Strategy and its Interplay with Innovation Ambidexterity Pay Off?
affiliations: University of Helsinki, University of East London, University of Vaasa, University of Reading, Charles Darwin University, University of Auckland Business School and University of Helsinki - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Does Differentiation Strategy and its Interplay with Innovation Ambidexterity Pay Off?
detail.abstract: The value of differentiation strategy is an iconic question in strategy, marketing, and innovation management. It can be approached from multiple perspectives, such as marketing-based, technology-based, and business model-based differentiation perspectives. Employing an organizational ambidexterity perspective, the present study explores the moderating role of innovation ambidexterity on the effect of differentiation strategy on firm market value. The study uses a unique measurement approach with two-ends-of-continuum (vs. orthogonal) of exploration and exploitation through machine learning, natural language processing, and computer-aided text analysis of annual reports. As a result, the current research proposes and finds an inverted U-shaped relationship, challenging the linear relationship findings in extant research of differentiation strategy and the firm market value, and an inverted U-shaped interaction between differentiation strategy and innovation ambidexterity on the firm market value. The importance of finding an optimal balance between differentiation strategy and innovation ambidexterity to maximize the positive impact on market value is highlighted for mangers. Our findings indicate the importance of balanced innovation ambidexterity to create financial value from a differentiation strategy.

title: When Algorithms are the Customer: Why Systemic Reliability Replaces Relational Capital

detail.title: When Algorithms are the Customer: Why Systemic Reliability Replaces Relational Capital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This working paper introduces 'systemic reliability' as a critical innovation capability for organizations competing in the era of algorithmic commerce. As AI-powered procurement systems and autonomous agents increasingly replace human buyers, the foundational logic of business-to-business commerce is undergoing a fundamental shift. I argue that reliance on relational capital-interpersonal trust and human networks-is becoming insufficient as a primary source of competitive advantage. In its place, a new imperative emerges: demonstrable and verifiable integrity of an organization's technical and operational systems. This paper develops a conceptual framework integrating relationship theory and platform economics to explain this transformation. I define systemic reliability, encompassing data integrity, API performance, and operational consistency, and propose the 'Innovation Systems Architect' as a new organizational archetype. This framework explains how value is created and which capabilities matter most when the customer is an algorithm.

title: Competing in the Age of Algorithmic Intermediation: A Dynamic Capabilities Framework for Algorithmic Readiness (Working Paper)

detail.title: Competing in the Age of Algorithmic Intermediation: A Dynamic Capabilities Framework for Algorithmic Readiness (Working Paper)

detail.abstract: As autonomous AI agents increasingly intermediate commercial transactions, organizations confront a fundamental strategic challenge: competing when algorithms, not humans, evaluate and select suppliers. We develop the construct of algorithmic readinessorganizational capacity to compete effectively in AI agent-mediated markets-grounded in dynamic capabilities theory. Through expert interviews with platform strategists and procurement executives, we identify distinctive capability requirements that extend beyond digital maturity. We theorize algorithmic readiness through sensing (detecting when algorithmic evaluation criteria diverge from human preferences), seizing (managing the transparency-protection paradox in data provision), and transforming (operating dual-mode systems for human and algorithmic audiences). We develop testable propositions linking algorithmic readiness to competitive outcomes, specify boundary conditions, and provide preliminary empirical validation. This research addresses critical gaps in understanding organizational adaptation when the nature of the "customer" fundamentally changes.

detail.abstract: The imposition of reciprocal tariffs by the United States government since 2025 has created unprecedented pressures on the healthcare delivery infrastructure, with particularly acute consequences for the physiotherapy sector. This research paper synthesizes current evidence regarding tariff-induced cost escalations across medical device procurement, pharmaceutical supply chains, and rehabilitation equipment distribution networks. Drawing from healthcare industry surveys, market analyses, and economic projections, we examine the multifaceted mechanisms through which tariff policies disrupt physiotherapy service delivery while simultaneously elevating treatment costs for patients and healthcare institutions. Our analysis demonstrates that 82% of healthcare administrators anticipate facility cost increases of 15% within six months of tariff implementation, with rehabilitation equipment expenditures rising between 18% and 25%[1][2]. The physiotherapy sector, valued at $8.78 billion in 2023 and projected to grow to $12.5 billion by 2030 at a 5.2% compound annual growth rate, now faces significant structural barriers to capital investment and equipment modernization[3]. This paper identifies evidence-based mitigation strategies, explores the economic mechanisms underlying cost transmission, and provides clinical and administrative recommendations for physiotherapy practices navigating the current tariff environment.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how exchange rate regime flexibility impacts the allocation of labor across firms. Specifically, we investigate how differences in labor-intensity or capitalintensity in production affect employment decisions under various degrees of exchange rate regime flexibility. In a simple theoretical model, we show that firms utilizing more laborintensive production technologies are more likely to expand their employment when the exchange rate they face becomes less flexible. In contrast, firms employing more capitalintensive technology tend to hire more workers when the exchange rate is more flexible. We test our theory using granular firm-level data from China and provide robust evidence supporting the theoretical predictions.

title: Quantitative Evaluation of Volatility-Adaptive Trend-Following Models in Cryptocurrency Markets

detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets exhibit extreme volatility, heavy-tailed return distributions, and structurally persistent inefficiencies arising from fragmented liquidity and heterogeneous market participants. In addition to posing a challenge to conventional portfolio theory, these features offer a special testing ground for momentum-based trading systems. This paper presents a trend-following framework that adjusts to volatility in high-frequency cryptocurrency markets, focusing on Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH). The proposed structure uses multi-horizon moving averages to detect trends. It uses a multi-timeframe Relative Strength Index (RSI) filter to confirm momentum and employs Average True Range (ATR) scaling to manage risk based on volatility. Trade exits are set by combining ATRbased trailing stops with Exponential Moving Average (EMA) slope reversal detection. This combination creates an exit system that balances staying in the trend while managing risk effectively. Furthermore, cross-correlation analysis reveals that BTC and ETH share a time-varying but persistently high correlation structure (ρ ≈ 0.8-0.9), suggesting common volatility regimes. This validates the use of joint parameter optimization across correlated assets as a robustness-enhancing constraint. Collectively, the findings indicate that volatility-adjusted, momentum-confirmed trendfollowing systems can generate statistically and economically significant excess returns in cryptocurrency markets, provided that their optimization framework is adaptive, crossvalidated, and sensitive to dynamic volatility states.

title: Environmental Regulations, Market Power in Input Markets, and the Labor Share
affiliations: Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management

detail.title: Environmental Regulations, Market Power in Input Markets, and the Labor Share
detail.abstract: This paper examines how environmental regulation reshapes firms' market power in input markets and alters the labor share. Using comprehensive Chinese manufacturing firm-level data, I document substantial market power in both labor and intermediate-input markets. Stricter environmental regulation increases wage markdowns by strengthening firms' monopsony power in local labor markets, while reducing materials markdowns as firms face higher input costs and reduced buyer power. Exploiting quasi-experimental variation from a major air pollution control policy, I show that these shifts in input wedges reallocate regulatory burdens: rising materials costs and increased monopsony power jointly lower labor's share of value added by approximately 9 percent. Counterfactual estimates indicate that, absent these input-market channels, the decline in China's manufacturing labor share since the early 2000s would have been 15 percent smaller. The results highlight that environmental policy interacts strongly with pre-existing input-market distortions, amplifying distributional consequences of the green transition.

detail.abstract: We present the generalized properties of gains from trade in monopolistic competition models featuring firm heterogeneity characterized by Pareto-distributed productivity and variable markups associated with the pro-competitive effect. Under an additively separable utility function with only the minimum assumptions required to describe this framework, we find that (i) the mass of consumed varieties can serve as a sufficient statistic for welfare gains from trade and that (ii) markup distortions in both closed and open economies can be characterized as a combination of optimal firm entry and underproduction (overproduction) by firms with relatively high (low) markups. Furthermore, (iii) contrary to the predictions under symmetric firm models, the pro-competitive effect of trade does not eliminate these markup distortions. With a Pareto distribution, international trade fails to close the welfare gap between the market equilibrium and optimum, generating no efficiency gains. This finding suggests that under firm heterogeneity, opening up to trade or trade liberalization cannot serve as effective means of eliminating markup distortions.

title: Leverage and Credit Risk Dynamics under Costly Equity Issuance
affiliations: Imperial College London, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Leverage and Credit Risk Dynamics under Costly Equity Issuance
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic game-theoretic model of leverage and credit risk pricing, featuring downward jump cash-flow shocks and costly external equity. The firm begins with a low target leverage and rolls over its debt at equilibrium interest rates, allowing leverage to drift in response to realized earnings. As leverage rises, the firm proactively deleverages through recapitalization, preserving financial slack and mitigating default risk. Default occurs unpredictably following a downward jump shock and becomes more likely as leverage increases, causing equilibrium credit spreads to rise with leverage. The firm is endogenously risk-averse at low leverage but becomes risk-seeking at high leverage.

title: How Investors Pick Stocks: Global Evidence from 1,540 AI-Driven Field Interviews

detail.title: How Investors Pick Stocks: Global Evidence from 1,540 AI-Driven Field Interviews
detail.abstract: We conduct AI-driven field interviews with 1,540 actual investors, including many "millionaires," across ten countries to examine how individuals pick stocks. Textual analysis of the transcripts uncovers thirteen recurrent mechanisms that together form an empirically grounded taxonomy of actual investor behavior. Several frequently invoked mechanisms are only partially reflected in current mainstream asset-pricing theories. We also document substantial heterogeneity both across and within investors: while some emphasize certain mechanisms, others rely on markedly different ones, and many draw simultaneously on multiple approaches. Our evidence points to the need for theoretical refinements that accommodate heterogeneous agents with distinct preferences and belief systems.

detail.abstract: Recent debate over the expiration of the enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credit has focused narrowly on subsidy levels rather than on the structure of the U.S. health insurance system itself. This paper argues that the affordability crisis in individual insurance markets reflects deeper design failures rather than insufficient public spending. It examines five structural weaknesses in the ACA framework: (1) the misalignment between Medicaid and exchange coverage for low-income households, (2) the inefficient treatment of children through private family plans instead of CHIP, (3) the distortionary effects of incomelinked subsidies, (4) the absence of explicit protection against catastrophic risk, and (5) the instability created by employment-based insurance. The analysis shows how current policy raises premiums, increases implicit marginal tax rates, and destabilizes coverage during economic downturns. The paper concludes that durable reform requires redirecting public subsidies away from blanket premium support and toward structural interventions that lower medical costs, reduce income-based distortions, and improve continuity of coverage.

detail.abstract:
Many nations around the globe made the decision at the beginning of 2020 to partially or entirely go online and close schools to limit the spread of coronavirus (COVID-19).
The present work describes the effect of the design of the e-assessment item on the assessment item and student performance in a private school system in Karachi, Pakistan. In compliance with e-assessment item writing guidelines, five e-assessment test items were developed and five e-assessment test items were designed that were imprecise and not according to e-assessment item writing guidelines. Between these two e-assessment items, the difference in item difficulty was assessed. It also compared the effect on student performance of standard (precise) and non-standard (imprecise) e-assessment products. E-assessment items that were non-standard or imprecise were 0.37 points more complicated than the standard or precise e-assessment items. In an MCQ style item and ambiguous stem, double negative statement emerged as the most relevant items on the item difficulty scale, i.e. 0.20 and 0.10, respectively. Mean student performance score was compared in both settings and a major difference was observed in the mean score of students when standard or correct mean e-assessment results were compared with imprecise or non-standard items, i.e. 17 and 9, respectively. The study therefore concludes that student performance was found to be more difficult and adversely affected by non-standard or imprecise e-assessment items. Therefore, for a legitimate and accurate e-assessment at schools, e-assessment item writing guidelines and principles should be addressed.

detail.abstract: This paper incorporates limited informational perspective taking into a class of sender-receiver games. The sender wants to distort the truth, but the receiver can verify her message at some privately known cost. A projecting receiver exaggerates the chance that the sender knows his type and tailors the truthfulness of her message to his cost. Such biased second-order beliefs introduce a wedge between the actual and perceived informativeness of the sender's message and lead to credulity and disbelief in equilibrium. If the con ‡ict is neither too large nor too small, and veri…cation is neither too easy nor too di¢ cult, persuasion is uniformly deceptive and receivers believe too much what senders want them to believe. Comparative statics are non-monotone and both a decrease in the con ‡ict and an increase in veri…cation costs systematically boost credulity and lower receiver welfare. When endogenizing the con ‡ict by bringing in the seller of the asset, I show that under unbiased beliefs, the seller's pro…t is maximal with no con ‡ict. Instead, under projection, a commonly-known con ‡ict allows the seller to extract maximal pro…t with the receiver always being credulous on average, …nancial literacy back…ring, and advice becoming toxic.

title: Immigrant Status and Housing Cost Strain in the United States: Evidence from the Global Flourishing Study
affiliations: Stanford University

detail.title: Immigrant Status and Housing Cost Strain in the United States: Evidence from the Global Flourishing Study
detail.abstract: Using over 70,000 respondents from the Global Flourishing Study (GFS) between 2023-24, I examine how immigrant status relates to financial anxiety in U.S. housing markets. I analyze two short-run stress outcomes: a binary indicator for reporting difficulty living on current income and a standardized index of worry about safety, food, and housing. First, I find that immigrants exhibit higher financial anxiety than otherwise similar natives. This gap is concentrated among renters and is negligible among homeowners. The tenure split is the most robust feature of the data: immigrant-native differences in stress are primarily a rentermarket phenomenon rather than a general housing-market effect. Second, I complement the household-level analysis with a county-level long-difference design that links changes in immigrant population shares to changes in rent-to-income ratios and house prices. Counties experiencing faster immigrant population growth display somewhat faster increases in housing costs, particularly in more tightly regulated markets, but these associations attenuate substantially once income and population growth are controlled for.

detail.title: The Global Minimum Tax, Investment Incentives and Asymmetric Tax Competition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the OECD's global minimum tax (GMT) in a formal model of tax competition between asymmetric countries. We consider both profit shifting and real responses of multinational enterprises, and highlight the role of the substance-based income exclusion (SBIE) in investment incentives and tax rate setting. The GMT reduces the true tax rate differential and benefits the large country, while the revenue effect is generally ambiguous for the small country. In the short run where tax rates are fixed, the GMT reduces the small country's revenue if profit shifting costs are low and increases it otherwise. In the long run where countries adjust tax rates, the GMT reshapes the tax game and the competition pattern. We reveal that the minimum rate binds the small country only if it is low. With the rise of the GMT rate, countries will set tax rates below the minimum to boost capital investments and collect top-up taxes. Simulations show that a moderate GMT rate can raise both countries' revenues and the large country's welfare in the long run. However, it may reduce the small country's welfare if the welfare weight of private income is high.

detail.abstract: The subject of anti-competitive land covenants has been an area of focus for New Zealand competition law in the last few years. Reforms to the Commerce Act 1986 have had important implications for land covenants and the New Zealand Commerce Commission has recently focused on anti-competitive land covenants to a significant degree. Recent case law involving anti-competitive land covenants has proceeded on the basis of admissions of breach by the defendants to Commerce Commission penalty actions. As a consequence, the recent case law does not provide detailed guidance as to how s 28 of the Commerce Act 1986 dealing with anti-competitive land covenants should apply. The recent case law also has a focus on anti-competitive purpose rather than actual anti-competitive effect. This article reviews how s 28 should properly be applied to assess whether land covenants are anti-competitive and discusses the factors that should be taken into account in that assessment. It suggests an approach that focuses on the overall impact of a covenant in a market as a whole, and an objective approach to purpose that avoids the application of s 28 to land covenants that have no real likelihood of causing meaningful anticompetitive effects. The article also suggests that recent amendments to the prohibitions on cartel conduct in the Commerce Act create a risk of deterring legitimate land covenants that do not meaningfully impact on competition in the market. The amendments do this by categorising certain land covenants that restrict the production or supply of particular goods or services as cartel conduct in breach of s 30 (and potentially as a criminal offence under s 82B) when the land on which the covenant is imposed is transferred to a competitor of the party who imposed the covenant. The article suggests that this is an overreach of competition law which should be rectified by statutory reform. The reform suggested is to ensure that land covenants that restrict the supply of goods or services only be considered unlawful where they breach s 28 and so have an impact on competition in a market as a whole.

title: Agricultural Cash Transfers and the Rise of Farm Employers: Evidence from Odisha's KALIA Program in India

detail.title: Agricultural Cash Transfers and the Rise of Farm Employers: Evidence from Odisha's KALIA Program in India
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether large agricultural cash transfers can change rural labor market composition. Using Labor Force Surveys from 1999-2000 to 2023-24 and a synthetic control design, we examine Odisha's KALIA program. We estimate that the share of employers in agricultural employment in Odisha rises by 3.6 percentage points relative to its synthetic control, a six-fold increase over pre-program levels, driven by declines in own-account farming. For policy, this suggests that unconditional cash transfers can support the emergence of small farm employers, but complementary access to credit, technology, and markets is likely needed if these transitions are to be durable.

title: The Impossibility of a Fixed-Limit Money: Bitcoin Fallacies

detail.title: The Impossibility of a Fixed-Limit Money: Bitcoin Fallacies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent Researcher
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
No item of a publicly known fixed-limit of supply has ever elevated to monetary status in an economically significant domain. Analysis of the spectrum of economic thought, spanning orthodox and heterodox approaches, reveals why such elevation is impossible. Hypothetical elevation of a fixed-limit item to monetary status results in economic collapse via extreme deflationary dynamics - hyperdeflation - wherein real and anticipated purchasing power appreciation encourages hoarding behavior, decimating aggregate demand, transaction velocity, and real output. 

Analysis of cryptocurrency literature written in support of fixed-limit digital money reveals misunderstanding of monetary requirements, the integrated functions of money, deflationary dynamics, and even fundamental monetary definitions. Such errors are exemplified in Saifedean Ammous's The Bitcoin Standard which points to the Austrian school for support, yet misrepresents its position. 

Common claims that the Bitcoin software produces "money" and "digital gold" are demonstrably false. The gold comparison fails through supply dynamics differential: gold provides supply elasticity through market-responsive production, while Bitcoin's predetermined supply cannot adjust to economic conditions. The Kaneda Curve demonstrates that price stability requires the anchoring of purchasing power expectations via an elastic money supply that responds to market signals. 

The certainty of economic collapse under a fixed-limit money system excludes Bitcoin from the category of money, invalidating derivative store of value claims with profound implications for investors and regulators.

title: Shifting Endpoints and the Information Effect of Monetary Policy
affiliations: Prague University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Shifting Endpoints and the Information Effect of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a learning channel of monetary policy transmission that reconciles declining long-term interest rates with their substantial policy sensitivity. We argue that monetary policy affects the economy by shaping agents’ beliefs about long-run fundamentals; that is, the learning channel alters policy effects through evolving expectations. We formalize the mechanism in an analytically tractable New Keynesian model with incomplete information and test it using high-frequency announcement surprises and smooth local projections for the US (1989–2023). The results show that the effects of monetary policy shocks are significantly influenced by concurrent movements in long-term yields.

title: Efficient and Sustainable Adaptation of Large Language Models via Entropy-Guided Subnetworks and Fractal Pruning

detail.title: Efficient and Sustainable Adaptation of Large Language Models via Entropy-Guided Subnetworks and Fractal Pruning
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deliver state-of-the-art performance across diverse NLP tasks, yet their deployment is constrained by high computational and storage costs. We present a two-stage framework that (1) selects a domain-adaptive subnetwork via entropy-guided neuron ranking and (2) compresses it using a structured Hausdorff-stable fractal pruning mask. Our rate-distortion optimized calibration yields accurate entropy estimates with only 500-1,000 samples. Experiments on SST-2, IMDb, SQuAD v1.1, and a public EU Law classification dataset demonstrate an average 83.7% reduction in FLOPs with ≤1.2% drop in test accuracy/F1 against full fine-tuning, outperforming LoRA, QLoRA, SpIEL, SparseGPT, Wanda, and E-Sparse.

title: Regenerative Cycle Architecture: A General Theory of Temporal Governance in Institutional Systems

detail.title: Regenerative Cycle Architecture: A General Theory of Temporal Governance in Institutional Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or case studies requiring ethics approval. No ethical approval was necessary for this theoretical and conceptual research.

detail.abstract:
Institutions frequently fail not because they lack resources or expertise, but because their capital cycles are structurally bound to short-horizon fragility cycles—financial volatility, political turnover, capability decay, and civic fluctuation. These fragility cycles operate on timescales fundamentally misaligned with the long-horizon mission cycles that govern asset lifetimes, scientific capability, climate adaptation, and intergenerational public goods. This temporal mismatch produces deterministic capability decline across domains, regardless of managerial competence or policy intent.

This paper introduces Regenerative Cycle Architecture (RCA), a general meta-theory of institutional design based on two structural operations: cycle decoupling, which renders capital independent of fragility cycles; and cycle alignment, which synchronises capital behaviour with mission cycles. RCA formalises a cycle ontology, a three-layer system architecture, and six structural invariants that are jointly sufficient for regenerative, multi-cycle institutional capability. The paper shows how RCA explains failure patterns across climate adaptation, science, infrastructure, health, and civic systems, and demonstrates that Perpetual Social Capital (PSC) constitutes the first realised implementation of RCA at the capital layer. RCA concludes by introducing the cycle constitution—a new constitutional category that protects temporal integrity in the same way political constitutions protect power.

The paper outlines an interdisciplinary research agenda for RCA as a foundational framework for long-horizon, regenerative institutional design.

detail.abstract: The National Educational Policy (NEP) 2020, introduced by the Government of India, marks a transformative milestone in the country's education landscape. The strategy intends to bridge the gap between academia and industries, cultivating a skilled and innovative workforce capable of driving economic growth and sustainable development, with a vision to overhaul the educational system to match the needs of the 21st-century workforce. This abstract explores the significant impact of NEP 2020 on industrial disciplines, focusing on key aspects that contribute to workforce readiness and industrial development. The policy places a strong emphasis on skill development, promoting vocational education, and integrating practical learning opportunities into the curriculum. By empowering students with industry-relevant skills, the NEP aims to address the longstanding skill gaps that have hindered India's workforce productivity.

title: Money, Markets, and Machines: The New Era of Finance

detail.title: Money, Markets, and Machines: The New Era of Finance
detail.abstract:
The world of finance has dramatically transformed from a slow-moving, institution-dominated system into a dynamic, technology-powered global arena where speed, data, and intelligence define success. What was once dependent on physical banks, paperwork, and limited access has now evolved into a borderless ecosystem driven by digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and automated market mechanisms. This research explores how the traditional principles of money and markets have been reshaped by machines, altering not only financial operations but also human behavior, decision-making, and power structures within the economy.

By tracing the journey from conventional finance to today’s hyper-connected financial landscape, this study reveals how the “game of finance” has fundamentally changed — shifting control from centralized institutions to technology-enabled individuals while simultaneously introducing new complexities and risks. It investigates the implications of this transformation for investors, institutions, and global economic stability, offering insight into how innovation has redefined wealth creation, financial accessibility, and strategic thinking. Ultimately, the paper presents a thought-provoking understanding of what this new era signifies and how society must adapt to thrive within this rapidly evolving financial reality.

title: The Missing "Loser's Curse": Experimental Evidence on Belief-Based Models in Common-Value Auctions
affiliations: University of Queensland - School of Economics and University of Queensland

detail.title: The Missing "Loser's Curse": Experimental Evidence on Belief-Based Models in Common-Value Auctions
detail.abstract: Models based on mistaken beliefs, such as Cursed Equilibrium and Level-k Thinking, are among the leading explanations for the Winner's Curse observed in common-value auctions. We argue that these models predict a Loser's Curse in other auctions formats. Using an experiment with a within-subject design, we test for the presence of both curses in uniform-price auctions with common values. At the aggregate level, we find evidence of a strong Winner's Curse, but no evidence of a Loser's Curse. These aggregate findings cast some doubts on the ability of beliefbased models to fully explain the Winner's Curse. Indeed, at the individual level, the behavior of most subjects is better described by Joy of Winning and Quantal Response Equilibrium. We also find suggestive evidence of failures of contingent thinking: subjects behave closer to the rational benchmark in a non-strategic task when the relevant contingency is made more salient.

title: Farmers' Responses to Temperature and Rainfall Shocks in Indonesia
affiliations: University of Washington, University of Seoul and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy

detail.title: Farmers' Responses to Temperature and Rainfall Shocks in Indonesia
detail.abstract: In the tropics, climate variability poses greater risks to agro-ecosystems than warming (Olonscheck et al., 2021; Vasseur et al., 2014). We study Indonesian farmers' responses to temperature and rainfall shocks, defined as deviations from local seasonal means. Exploiting within-subdistrict variation over time, we find that both unusually high and low temperatures reduce rural household expenditure, while low rainfall does not. Households buffer these shocks by drawing down liquid assets and increasing agricultural work hours. Low rainfall shifts hours from non-agricultural to agricultural work, whereas temperature shocks increase agricultural hours without reducing non-agricultural work. Farmers also adjust cultivated land area and crop mix. These results suggest that farmers intensify farming labor to mitigate weather-related losses, challenging the view that rural labor readily reallocates to non-agriculture during agricultural downturns, and indicate greater vulnerability to temperature variations than to rainfall.

title: The Universal Numerical Protocol (UNP): A Post-Fiat Framework for Ethical Value Representation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Universal Numerical Protocol (UNP): A Post-Fiat Framework for Ethical Value Representation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No relationship.

detail.abstract: This work introduces the Universal Numerical Protocol (UNP), a theoretical and computational model for representing and circulating economic value in a post-fiat context. Unlike fiat currencies (issued as debt) and cryptocurrencies (characterized by artificial scarcity and speculative dynamics), the UNP grounds value in the interaction between usage semantics, ethical algorithms, and a verifiable numerical structure. The architecture includes the issuance of Non-Debt Value Numbers (NVs), an Ethical Non-Liquid Asset (ENA), and a semantic engine for transaction validation. The model has been tested through simulations of digital city-states and compared with existing approaches such as MMT, CBDCs, public debt tokenization, and blockchain finance. Results highlight the UNP's potential to provide a fair, resilient, and redistributive monetary structure capable of redefining the very concept of money.

title: Spectral Clustering-Powered Survival Analysis for heterogeneous clinical datasets: a case study on COVID-19
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Trieste, University of Trieste, University of Trieste, University of Trieste, University of Trieste - Cattinara Hospital, University of Trieste, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Spectral Clustering-Powered Survival Analysis for heterogeneous clinical datasets: a case study on COVID-19
detail.abstract: Background and Objective:Heterogeneity and limited size are common challenges in health research datasets, as well as in several other fields, impacting the applicability of sophisticated machine learning algorithms for performing survival analysis.We propose a novel technique to identify and characterize subpopulations with differing survival behaviors in tabular datasets of modest sizes (i.e., up to thousands of samples), combining classical survival landmark analysis techniques with spectral clustering. Methods:Our technique consists in (1) extracting static and time-dependent features from the data, (2) partitioning the population with spectral clustering at relevant time landmarks, and (3) comparing the resulting subpopulations in terms of Kaplan-Meier survival curves, Cox's hazard ratios, and features distributions, by statistical testing.We employed the proposed technique to perform a retrospective inferential analysis on a dataset comprising information about 944 COVID-19 patients. Results:By applying this pipeline onto our dataset, we successfully identified two risk groups with statistically  distinct survival profiles and feature distributions across all landmark times, furthermore detailing when these differences manifest more prominently.Conclusions:The presented technique enables spotting survival patterns in challenging clinical datasets, which frequently arise in field research. While simple in principle, its application relies on manual tuning operated by fields experts. Furthermore, its demonstrated efficacy in inferential analysis could be easily extended to prediction. Future studies are required to validate its applicability on other datasets.

detail.abstract: Financial decisions are one of the most transformative decisions people make, carrying enough potential to alter their course of life. While various studies explore cognitive biases like overconfidence bias or confirmation bias, few examine how specific brain regions react during actual fintech interactions and their relation with poor risk management or system failure. Because of cognitive constraints and a low level of financial literacy, many individuals infringe sound financial principles. In the evolution of financial psychology, the term "neurofinance" coined by David Edwards in 2004, emerged integrating neurotechnology with financial behavior. The concept of neurofinance has developed out of neuroeconomics and has become the foundation for recent studies that examine the relationship between financial decisions and their effect on the human brain. The present study outlines the relation between cognitive traps and their implications in neurofinance, and it is expected to nurture further studies done for analyzing an individual's investment behavior and decision, with the concern of building the foundation and exploring Neurofinance in the field of behavioral finance research.

title: Assessment of Efficacy of Implementation of Capacity Building Measures under Kenya's Climate Change Law Regime: Conclusions and Recommendations
affiliations: University of Nairobi, University of Nairobi and University of Nairobi

detail.title: Assessment of Efficacy of Implementation of Capacity Building Measures under Kenya's Climate Change Law Regime: Conclusions and Recommendations
detail.abstract: Kenya has a higher vulnerability to climate change, which ranks it at 151 globally out of 181 in the 2019 ND-GAIN Index, due to its position and location in the Horn of Africa. It is projected that more rain, worse droughts and the emergence of drug-resistant diseases will be experienced in the coming decades, especially over the next 30 years, if little is done to improve resilience and adaptive capacity. On this basis, capacity building, among other measures, has been recommended as an enabler of climate change action, including resilience building. Guided by Hans Kelsen’s legal positivism theory, this study sought to assess how capacity-building measures have been included and implemented under Kenya’s climate change law regime, with Kisumu County serving as a case study. The study covered four areas: (1) assessment of capacity building mandates, (2) how various climate change actors are fulfilling their mandates, (3) barriers and opportunities and (4) options for strengthening capacity development. The data collection exercise involved the review of literature and key informant interviews. A purposeful sampling procedure was used to identify participants. The study established that capacity building is progressing moderately at institutional, systemic and individual levels. Legal frameworks exist, institutions have been established, and actors are active, but with varied capacities and approaches to capacity building. There exist challenges too: limited finances, inadequate skills, low awareness, weak coordination, lack of incentives, limited data and competition among global institutions. As we advance, the study recommends the development of a locally-led, need-based, multi-sector, and multi-stakeholder framework for capacity building for climate action at national and county levels.

title: Feedback on the EU’s European Research Act
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Feedback on the EU’s European Research Act
detail.abstract: Recombinant DNA technology, also known as mRNA technology, is a subset of genetic modification used in a variety of fields for many purposes. One of the most notable uses for mRNA technology is for the creation of vaccines, such as the vaccine used in the COVID-19 epidemic. This method of vaccine creation is arguably simpler and safer than traditional methods, but it still needs development to make it a viable method for the creation of all vaccines from now on. However, the research industry in Europe has been lacking in comparison to other areas of the world for years. It is consistently underinvested in when compared to other industries, limiting its growth. More importantly, there is an alarming shortage of skilled professionals willing to work in research. Recently, the EU has put forward the European Research Area (ERA) Act, which should serve to remedy this. MediQuills recommends that the ERA Act alters certain regulatory frameworks to encourage industry growth and help more STEM research be done in less time. MediQuills also supports creating specifications to encourage mRNA technology development as it will simplify the creation of lifesaving medication that could improve public health and help end public health crises like pandemics. Supporting scientific research also improves job prospects in the field, resulting in an increase of interest in research and STEM as a whole. When done in tandem with the establishment of educational programs to develop skills necessary for mRNA technology, this should help establish a dedicated workforce that will help expand the field further. MediQuills believes that with these additions, the ERA Act can revive Europe’s research industry and possibly even contribute to saving lives.

title: The Empire that Learned to Disappear: Why America Won’t Fall — It Will Fade
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: The Empire that Learned to Disappear: Why America Won’t Fall — It Will Fade
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the perceived decline of the United States does not signal collapse but metamorphosis-a gradual shift from being an industrial empire to a leader in information and finance. By comparing the United States with the British and Roman empires and examining China's structural limitations in geography, culture, and diplomacy, this study asserts that the U.S. remains the world's key organizing power. Although the American system is internally weakening, it continues to lead globally through language, currency, culture, and institutional stability. China's rise, while impressive, cannot replicate or replace the soft-power foundation that supports U.S. dominance. The paper concludes that modern empires no longer fall; they fade away-dispersing into networks, data, and ideology long after their industrial bases decline.

title: Taxation on Gifts and Windfall Gains: Where Should the Line of Income be Drawn?

detail.title: Taxation on Gifts and Windfall Gains: Where Should the Line of Income be Drawn?
detail.abstract: The taxation of gifts and windfall gains raises fundamental questions about fairness, ability to pay, and the limits of state power in private generosity. While income is traditionally defined by periodicity, effort, and expectation, gifts and sudden windfalls blur this boundary by being unearned yet financially significant. This paper critically examines how India and the United Kingdom have drawn this line-between taxable income and exempt benevolence through statutory design and judicial interpretation. Indian law, particularly Section 56(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, seeks a middle path by taxing non-relative gifts and windfalls while exempting familial and ceremonial transfers. In contrast, the United Kingdom relies heavily on inheritance taxation but leaves windfalls largely untouched. Drawing on comparative jurisprudence and international scholarship, the paper argues that India's calibrated framework better harmonises equity, administrative efficiency, and cultural realities. Ultimately, the legitimacy of tax policy depends not only on fiscal rationale but on social acceptance of where the line of income is drawn.

title: Reducing Petty Corruption in Healthcare with Insurance Literacy: Experimental Evidence from Ghana
affiliations: , University of Ghana - Department of Finance and ETH Zürich

detail.title: Reducing Petty Corruption in Healthcare with Insurance Literacy: Experimental Evidence from Ghana
detail.abstract: Despite having health insurance, patients in low-income countries like Ghana often face significant out-of-pocket health expenditures (OOPE) for covered services and drugs. This study examines whether a targeted information campaign can empower patients to reduce these unauthorized fees, especially in contexts of low health insurance literacy. Through a randomized controlled trial across 41 health facilities and 2,284 patients, we find that informing insured patients about their benefits increases their understanding of health insurance and leads to a 25% reduction in OOPE. The specific delivery method of the information (verbal vs. verbal and written, general vs. specific information) does not differentially affect outcomes, with all information messages being similarly effective. Importantly, this intervention does not compromise access to or the quality of healthcare. The results imply that information provision leads to a reduction in individual-level rent-seeking rather than facility-level cost recovery. While the results are encouraging, they also reveal a persistent challenge: 65% of insured patients still incur OOPE, underscoring that patient education alone is insufficient to fully eliminate the problem. Our study provides strong evidence for a simple, cost-effective intervention to combat petty corruption and improve financial protection in healthcare.

title: Revisiting the Phillips Curve in Bangladesh: An Empirical Investigation of the Inflation-Unemployment Trade-off (1991-2024)
affiliations: Comilla University

detail.title: Revisiting the Phillips Curve in Bangladesh: An Empirical Investigation of the Inflation-Unemployment Trade-off (1991-2024)
detail.abstract: The main goal of this study is to check if the Phillips Curve applies in Bangladesh. The Phillips Curve suggests that there might be a relationship where higher inflation is linked with lower unemployment. To do this, the study used econometric methods, including the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bound test model, to look at both short-term and long-term connections. First, the researchers performed the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) and Phillips-Perron (PP) tests to see if the data was stable. Then, they used the ARDL bound test to explore if there was a co-integration relationship between inflation and unemployment. The bounds testing results indicate that there is no long-run cointegrating relationship among the variables. The short-run coefficients of inflation and GDP growth were negative but statistically insignificant, suggesting that neither inflation nor economic growth has a meaningful short-term effect on unemployment in Bangladesh. Diagnostic and stability tests confirmed the model's reliability and parameter stability. These findings imply that the classical Phillips Curve trade-off between inflation and unemployment does not hold in the Bangladeshi context during the study period.

detail.abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (AI) transforms the work of financial analysts. Using the 2023 launch of FACTSET's AI platform as a natural experiment, we find that adoption produces markedly richer and more comprehensive reports-featuring 40% more distinct information sources, 34% broader topical coverage, and 25% greater use of advanced analytical methods-while also improving timeliness. Placebo tests using other data vendors confirm that these effects are unique to FACTSET's AI integration. Overall, our findings reveal both the productivity gains and cognitive limits of generative AI in financial information production.

title: How has Resource Abundance Influenced Income Inequality in Central Asia? A Case Study of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan

detail.title: How has Resource Abundance Influenced Income Inequality in Central Asia? A Case Study of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan
detail.abstract:
As the world is becoming more and more globalized, income inequality seems to be a relevant issue to the world. In fact, it is speculated that the top 1% of the adult earners in the world will hold 45.8% of all wealth in the world in 2020. Central Asia is no stranger to this problem. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Central Asian countries, as well as many other former Soviet Union members, saw a huge spike in income inequality across the region. This research tests whether one of the key qualities of the Central Asian countries – resource abundance – has contributed to income inequality in the region. 

The research has first identified how resource abundance (measured by resource rent-to-GDP-ratio) causes income inequality and what other factors could have caused income inequality in the region. Then, the data was gathered for each factor for available years and was run in a country-level linear regression model to see the relationship between resource abundance and income inequality. After that, it tested how consistent it is with past research to identify potential causality.

The research has concluded that for Kazakhstan, resource abundance seems to have little influence on income inequality, and the major cause is institutional quality. For Kyrgyz Republic, there’s actually a negative relationship, indicating that higher resource abundance is associated with lower income inequality, mainly due to lower average resource abundance and higher social spending. For the rest of the countries, accurate conclusions couldn’t have been drawn, mainly due to lack of proper data for the countries.

title: Rewiring Gender Norms: Causal Evidence on Internet Exposure and Justification of Intimate Partner Violence

detail.title: Rewiring Gender Norms: Causal Evidence on Internet Exposure and Justification of Intimate Partner Violence
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the causal impact of women's exposure to the internet on their attitudes towards intimate partner violence (IPV) using data from the most recent round of the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5). To address potential endogeneity, we exploit exogenous variation in district-level mobile tower density in India as an instrument for women's internet exposure. The instrumental variables estimation provides robust evidence that a woman's exposure to internet reduces her likelihood of justifying IPV by 21 percentage points. We also provide suggestive evidence that higher awareness and physical mobility are potential mechanisms through which internet exposure shapes attitudes. Our findings highlight the transformative potential of digital connectivity in challenging regressive gender norms.

title: From Corporate Misalignment to Market Failure: The Convergence Parallel and AI Governance in Sales & Marketing Systems

detail.title: From Corporate Misalignment to Market Failure: The Convergence Parallel and AI Governance in Sales & Marketing Systems
detail.abstract:
While AI safety discourse fixates on speculative superintelligence risks, commercial AI systems deployed today in sales and marketing already exhibit the instrumental convergence behaviors that researchers warn about. This paper introduces the "Convergence Parallel" framework, demonstrating structural homologies between corporate optimization and AI safety concerns. Through analysis of algorithmic price discrimination, manipulative interface design, and engagement-maximizing recommendation systems, we show how market-deployed AI manifests self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal-content integrity drives.

These instrumental behaviors create systematic market failures: information asymmetries, exploiting consumer cognitive biases, switching costs, locking in customers, and network effects, concentrating market power. The primary AI alignment problem in commercial contexts is institutional rather than technical—commercial AI functions exactly as designed, optimizing for objectives (revenue, engagement, conversion) that systematically diverge from consumer welfare.

Effective governance requires institutional intervention: market structure regulation addressing network effects, mandatory algorithmic transparency exposing exploitation, consumer protection modernization treating manipulation as per se unfair, and fundamental redesign aligning commercial incentives with human welfare. The Convergence Parallel framework reveals that AI alignment and institutional reform are unified challenges requiring coordinated political solutions.

title: Measuring Disagreement Beyond the Mean: A Density-Based Mutli-Metric Approach
affiliations: University of Lausanne

detail.title: Measuring Disagreement Beyond the Mean: A Density-Based Mutli-Metric Approach
detail.abstract: This paper introduces an extended framework for measuring forecaster disagreement using individual density forecasts and a range of distributional metrics, moving beyond traditional point-based measures. These densitybased metrics capture differences in individual forecast distributions, accounting for the second moment (variance) as well as higher-order moments (skewness, kurtosis), often overlooked in conventional metrics. Using ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters data, we show that density-based measures share broad patterns with point disagreement but capture deeper aspects of dispersion, showing greater sensitivity to macroeconomic uncertainty and policy shifts. We find that density-based disagreement is primarily driven by first and second moment components, with the role of the second moment becoming increasingly important over time. These measures also correlate more strongly with financial market volatility indicators, such as the VSTOXX.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of "Equilibri" a program designed to support mothers of children under 18 in Italy’s Piedmont region. The program is specifically aimed to help women who have reduced or stopped working due to motherhood to achieve better work-life balance by improving both employment and work-family outcomes. The evaluation, conducted via randomized control trial, shows positive impacts on employment and work-family balance. Women in the treatment group participated in professional courses, informal meetings, reconciliation support and extracurricular activities for their children. According to the results of our evaluation the program had a positive impact on mothers’ employment, work-life balance as well as children well-being. Furthermore, a greater proportion of women in the treatment group expressed a desire to have another child.

detail.abstract:
Published Book... Author: Azhar ul Haque Sario 

Atrial Fibrillation (AF) remains the most common and persistent cardiac arrhythmia, representing a significant global health burden associated with stroke and heart failure. Despite advancements in medical technology, traditional therapeutic approaches often rely on empirical, anatomical strategies—essentially treating the heart as a mechanical pump with plumbing issues. This reliance on "anatomical ablation" frequently results in high recurrence rates, as it fails to address the underlying non-linear dynamics driving the electrical chaos. This book, The Mathematics of the Heart, fills a critical void in current medical literature by bridging the disconnect between clinical electrophysiology and advanced applied mathematics. It proposes a fundamental paradigm shift: treating the heart not merely as a biological organ, but as a complex electrical grid governed by rigorous laws of physics and geometry.

The text provides a comprehensive framework for solving the "current disease problem" by translating biological behavior into solvable equations. It begins by utilizing the Monodomain Reaction-Diffusion equation to model the continuous spread of voltage, replacing the simplified view of cellular wiring with a more accurate "functional syncytium" model. The book details how the instability of the heartbeat—the genesis of the arrhythmia—can be predicted using Restitution Curves and the Weiss-Garfinkel condition, offering a mathematical explanation for the transition from a steady beat to a chaotic spiral. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of Topological Charge and Phase Singularities to identify "Rotors," the spinning electrical tornadoes that sustain AF, changing the clinical target from random noise to specific topological defects.

Unlike standard medical textbooks that focus on procedural technique, or pure engineering texts that lack clinical context, this work integrates these disciplines to offer actionable insights. It demonstrates how the Eikonal-Curvature equation explains the slowing of electrical waves in curved tissue, and how Shannon Entropy can be used to decode complex fractionated electrograms, distinguishing between the "noise" of passive tissue and the "signal" of active drivers. The book further differentiates itself by applying Fractal Geometry to quantify the roughness of cardiac fibrosis and utilizing Graph Theory—specifically the Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem—to design optimal ablation strategies that terminate arrhythmias with surgical precision.

For researchers and clinicians, this book offers a blueprint for the future of "Topological Medicine." It culminates in the application of Bayesian Inference and Digital Twins, advocating for the use of patient-specific computational models to simulate and test interventions in silico before physical implementation. By moving cardiology from an era of probabilistic guessing to one of deterministic mathematical certainty, this book provides the theoretical and practical tools necessary to master the physics of the heart, offering a new path toward curing the incurable.

title: Banks’ Regulatory Risk Tolerance

detail.abstract: We employ 68 quarters of data – including from non-public supervisory sources – to study how 17 US and 17 euro-area banks balance the risk of breaching regulatory requirements against the cost of maintaining and speedily restoring “management” buffers. We find that steady-state management buffer targets systematically declined and regulatory risk tolerance (RRT) rose following the Great Financial Crisis, especially at banks experiencing a stronger increase in capital requirements. As a sign that RRT is a conscious choice, banks facing more volatile management buffer shocks set higher management buffer targets. High-RRT banks tend to respond to a depletion of their management buffers by cutting lending, whereas low-RRT banks reduce the riskiness but not the volume of their assets — thus highlighting real-economy effects of capital management strategies.
